sentences.text: Hello, Margaret? It's Priya. Priya Nair, from adult social care. We spoke on the phone on Monday.
Oh yes, yes, come in love, come in. Mind the step, it's a bit high that one.
Well I've got the heating on. I know I shouldn't, not this time of year, but I feel the cold now, I really do.
It's that wind off the fields at the back. Go through, go through to the front room.
Sit anywhere. Well, not that one, that's the cat's. You can if you like but you'll get hairs all over you.
He's gorgeous. Look at him, he's not bothered by me at all.
He likes visitors. More than I do some days. Can I get you a cup of tea?
Oh, I'd love one, but only if it's not too much trouble. With your wrist, I mean.
No, no, the kettle I can manage. It's the big pans I can't do. Milk and sugar?
Just milk, please. Thank you.
Before we start properly, can I just explain what today is about?
Yes please, because Kevin said somebody was coming but I didn't really know what for.
That's alright, that's really common. So the hospital sent us a referral when you were discharged.
And the reason I'm here is to do what's called a needs assessment. It's under the Care Act.
It basically means we have a chat, and I try and understand how you're managing day to day. What's difficult, what's working, and, most importantly, what matters to you.
I see.
It'll probably take about an hour, if that's okay with you? And we can stop for a break whenever you want.
I've got nowhere to be, love. Only my quiz programme at four o'clock.
I never get any of the answers. I shout at the telly though.
Okay. We can come back to anything, anytime. And you mentioned Kevin. That's your son?
I don't want to be, um. I don't want to be put anywhere. If that's what this is.
No. And that's a really important thing to say, so thank you for saying it. This isn't about putting you anywhere.
It's about you, here, in your home, and what might make things easier for you.
Right. Well. That's alright then.
I'll be jotting a few notes as we go, is that alright?
My handwriting's gone to pot since this, so you're better off doing it.
Everything we talk about is confidential. But if I was worried that you or somebody else was at risk of harm, I might need to share that with other people.
But I'd always try and talk to you about it first. Is that okay?
Yes. Yes, that's fine.

Yes, I've got nothing to hide. Well. Mostly.
Take no notice of me. Go on.

Yes, he's my son. He said he'd try and come over, he's on an early shift, so he might pop in after he finishes.
Half eleven maybe.
Lovely. Well if he does come, we can include him, if you're happy with that.
He'll want to put his tuppence in, he always does.
Ha. Okay. So shall we start with the fall? Can you tell me in your own words what happened?
Well. It was the third of March. A Monday. I remember because the bin men had been.

First, me. Today I'll make the referral to occupational therapy.

The OT waiting list is about three weeks at the moment. I'll mark it as a priority because of the falls, but I can't promise it'll be quicker.
Second, I'll make the safeguarding referral about the card, this afternoon, like we said. Somebody from the safeguarding team will be in touch with you, Margaret, and I'll be in touch as well.
Alright.
Third, I'll write to Dr Shah. I'll ask about a referral to the falls clinic, and I'll mention the weight loss, the continence service, and the missed tablets.
